completion_conditions: A target installed into an empty directory passes its own validate, its own unittest discovery, and every shipped contract test.
A static check fails when a shipped artifact depends on something unshipped.
No file from .shiki/leases or any other runtime-local directory reaches a target.
An upgrade updates the governance contracts or reports exactly what it could not update; per-project content is never destroyed unprompted.
A target records which Shiki it was installed from, and doctor reports drift against it.
The full suite, the init/doctor/control-plane suites and validate_shiki stay green.

decisions: A fresh install cannot pass its own `Validate Shiki mirror` check, and four independent causes were measured. `TEMPLATE_PATHS` has 77 entries; `tests` is not among them, yet the SHIPPED `.github/workflows/shiki-validate.yml:31` runs `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` with no guard. `scripts/shiki_session_lease.py` is not shipped, yet the SHIPPED `scripts/test_shiki_runner_claude.sh` imports it. `scripts/shiki_contract_approval.py` is not shipped, yet the SHIPPED `scripts/test_shiki_guardian_policy.sh` asserts its behaviour. `.gitignore` is not shipped at all.

The installer copies the platform's LIVE session lease into every new target. Measured by calling `should_skip` directly: `.shiki/leases/x.lock` -> skip=False, while `.shiki/ledger/L-1.json` -> skip=True and `.shiki/gha/pr.json` -> skip=True. The mirror history is correctly filtered because those directories are in the manifest's `create_directories`; `.shiki/leases` was added to the manifest when the session lease landed but never added there. The copied lock then names a task id from a DIFFERENT repository and, with no `.gitignore` shipped, gets committed.

The class matters more than the four instances: nothing checks that a file a SHIPPED artifact depends on is itself shipped. The durable fix is a static completeness check over the shipping surface, plus an install-and-verify test — not four one-off additions.

The documented upgrade is a no-op. `docs/operations.md:72-74` says re-running the bootstrap is idempotent and never mentions `--force`; `--force` is `store_true` (default False) at `scripts/shiki_cli.py:42` and `:100`, and `copy_path` warns `kept existing file:` and returns for every path that already exists. An operator following the docs sees exit 0 and hundreds of `kept existing file` warnings, and nothing is updated.

`--force`, the only upgrade that works, preserves and destroys exactly the wrong sets. `PRESERVE_UNDER_FORCE` is `('.shiki/guardian-policy.json', '.shiki/config.yaml', '.shiki/migrations/state.json')`. So the two files that carry the governance contract — the required-check list that becomes branch protection, and the approval-source list — are the ones an upgrade never updates, while `CONTEXT.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.github/CODEOWNERS`, which carry per-project content, are overwritten with template text, unprompted and unbacked-up.

Neither direction may simply be flipped. Overwriting `config.yaml` would destroy target-specific values; preserving it silently is what produces the undetectable half-upgrade. The resolution is to write the incoming version alongside as `<file>.new` and report the difference, so nothing is lost and nothing is silently stale.

Nothing records a version. `'VERSION' in TEMPLATE_PATHS` is False, no Python file reads `VERSION`, and `shiki status` emits only `claude_command, codex_skill, command, config, root`. An old target is internally consistent, so `validate_shiki` passes and `doctor` reports zero failures — the absence of a version is why a stale target is indistinguishable from a current one.

Deleting files that upstream removed (an obsolete workflow that keeps posting a check context) is deliberately OUT of scope. A prune pass is a destructive operation on a target repository and needs its own decision and its own approval; adding it here would put an unreviewed delete in the same change as the fixes that make install work at all.
grill_with_docs.source: Measured 2026-08-03 against main at 93cf467 by driving shiki_installer directly and by inspecting the shipped artifacts.

non_goals: Pruning files that upstream removed — destructive, needs its own decision.
Changing what any gate enforces, or any schema.
Changing the loop, the CCA, or MergeGate.
Silently overwriting a target's own .shiki/config.yaml or .shiki/guardian-policy.json.
Touching any file outside the declared locks.
outcome: A repository installed from this Shiki can pass its own required checks, can be upgraded without silently keeping stale governance or destroying per-project content, and can be asked what version it has. Today none of these hold: a fresh install is permanently red under the branch protection the installer itself applies, the documented upgrade is a no-op, and nothing anywhere records a version.

tasks.scope:
Close the four measured gaps AND the class that produced them.

The four gaps: add `tests` and `.gitignore` to `TEMPLATE_PATHS`; add `scripts/shiki_session_lease.py` and `scripts/shiki_contract_approval.py` to `TEMPLATE_PATHS`; and stop copying `.shiki/leases` into a target — the natural fix is to register `.shiki/leases` in the manifest the same way the other runtime-local state directories are registered, so `should_skip` filters it for the same reason it already filters `.shiki/ledger` and `.shiki/gha`. Whatever mechanism is chosen, a lock file must never reach a target and must never be committable there.

The class: add `tests/test_install_completeness.py` with a STATIC check over the shipping surface. For every shipped Python module under `scripts/`, every shipped `scripts/test_shiki_*.sh`, and every shipped `.github/workflows/*.yml`, resolve the repository-relative artifacts it depends on — Python imports of sibling `shiki_*` modules, `scripts/...` and `tests/...` paths referenced in shell and YAML, and the directory a `unittest discover -s <dir>` names — and assert each is either in `TEMPLATE_PATHS` or on an EXPLICIT, commented exception list. The exception list must be a named constant with a reason per entry, so an omission is a deliberate recorded decision rather than an oversight. This is the check that would have caught all four gaps at once.

Add an install-and-verify case to `scripts/test_shiki_init.sh`: install into a fresh temporary directory, then, from inside that directory, run the target's own `python3 scripts/validate_shiki.py`, `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`, and every shipped `scripts/test_shiki_*.sh`, asserting zero failures. Assert also that `.shiki/leases` is absent or empty in the installed target and that the installed `.gitignore` ignores it. This test is the acceptance for the whole task: if a fresh install cannot pass its own required checks, it fails.

REPRODUCIBILITY — what this task removes, and what to change to get the same result.
  Symptom: `shiki init` prints `target Shiki validation passed` and exits 0. The operator now has a repository whose every PR is permanently red on `Validate Shiki mirror` — and because `init` also applied branch protection requiring that check, nothing in that repository can ever merge.
  Measured 2026-08-03 against main at 93cf467: `TEMPLATE_PATHS` has 77 entries. `'tests' in TEMPLATE_PATHS` -> False, while the shipped `.github/workflows/shiki-validate.yml:31` runs `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`. `'scripts/shiki_session_lease.py' in TEMPLATE_PATHS` -> False, while the shipped `scripts/test_shiki_runner_claude.sh` imports that module. `'scripts/shiki_contract_approval.py' in TEMPLATE_PATHS` -> False, while the shipped `scripts/test_shiki_guardian_policy.sh` asserts its behaviour. `'.gitignore' in TEMPLATE_PATHS` -> False.
  Fourth cause, measured by calling the installer's own filter: `should_skip(ROOT/'.shiki/leases/x.lock', target_install=True)` -> False, versus True for `.shiki/ledger/L-1.json` and `.shiki/gha/pr.json`. The mirror directories are filtered because they appear in the manifest's `create_directories` list; `.shiki/leases` does not appear there. The platform's live lock — naming a task id from another repository — is therefore copied in, and with no `.gitignore` shipped it is committed.
  Why a static completeness check and not four additions: all four are the same defect — a shipped artifact depending on something unshipped, with nothing checking the relationship. Adding four paths fixes today and not tomorrow.
  Reproducible when: a fresh install passes its own validate, its own unittest discovery, and every shipped contract test, and the completeness check fails if any shipped artifact gains an unshipped dependency.

tasks.scope:
Replace the two-way preserve/overwrite split with a three-way one, so nothing is lost and nothing is silently stale.
  - PROJECT CONTENT — `CONTEXT.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.github/CODEOWNERS` — is never overwritten, even under `--force`. The incoming template is written alongside as `<file>.new` and reported, so the operator can merge deliberately.
  - GOVERNANCE CONTRACT — `.shiki/config.yaml`, `.shiki/guardian-policy.json` — is likewise never silently kept: write `<file>.new` alongside and report a per-key summary of what differs, naming `mergegate.required_checks` and `approval_sources` explicitly because those two decide what branch protection requires and what can approve. `.shiki/migrations/state.json` stays preserved outright — it is target history, not a contract.
  - EVERYTHING ELSE is overwritten under `--force`, as today.
The run must print, at the end, a single explicit summary of every `.new` written, so a half-upgrade is visible rather than inferred.

Move the precondition checks AHEAD of any file write. Measured order today: `install_template` — which validates INSIDE itself — runs at `scripts/shiki_bootstrap.py:235`, before `write_target_repo_config`, `commit_manifest`, `push_branch`, `configure_claude_code_secret` and `protect_branch`. A target with pending migrations therefore has its tree rewritten and then the run aborts before commit, push, secret and branch protection. Validate first; write nothing until the preconditions pass.

Document `--force` in `docs/operations.md` and `docs/releasing.md` as the required flag for an upgrade, replacing the current claim that re-running the bootstrap is idempotent, and document the `.new` convention.

Replace the hardcoded `CODEOWNERS_REQUIRED_OWNER = "@mizutani-140"` in `scripts/shiki_contracts.py` with a value resolved per target, so a repository owned by anyone else can satisfy its own CODEOWNERS check. Keep the current value as the default for this repository.

Add `tests/test_install_force_semantics.py`: without `--force` nothing existing changes (the current behaviour, pinned); with `--force`, each of the four project-content files keeps its content and gains a `.new`; each of the two governance files keeps its content, gains a `.new`, and is named in the summary; `migrations/state.json` gains no `.new` and is untouched; every other file is overwritten; a target with pending migrations is refused with NO file written — asserted by content hashing the tree before and after; and the CODEOWNERS owner is target-resolved, proved with a fixture naming a different owner.

REPRODUCIBILITY — what this task removes, and what to change to get the same result.
  Symptom 1: the operator follows `docs/operations.md:72-74`, re-runs the bootstrap, sees exit 0 and hundreds of `kept existing file:` warnings, and believes the target is upgraded. Nothing changed. The stale gate keeps running and keeps reporting green.
  Measured: `--force` is `store_true` with default False (`scripts/shiki_cli.py:42`, `:100`); `copy_path` returns after warning `kept existing file:` when the destination exists and `force` is false. `--force` appears nowhere in `docs/operations.md` or `docs/releasing.md`.
  Symptom 2: the operator discovers `--force`, and it overwrites `CONTEXT.md` — the glossary AGENTS.md names as the source of truth for domain language — plus `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.github/CODEOWNERS`, with no prompt and no backup, while keeping `.shiki/config.yaml` and `.shiki/guardian-policy.json`.
  Measured: `PRESERVE_UNDER_FORCE == ('.shiki/guardian-policy.json', '.shiki/config.yaml', '.shiki/migrations/state.json')`; everything else is copied over.
  Why that split is exactly backwards: `config.yaml` carries `mergegate.required_checks`, which `shiki init --protect` pushes to GitHub as the branch-protection contexts. A gate job added upstream therefore runs in the upgraded target, posts its check, can go red — and blocks nothing, because the preserved config never listed it. `guardian-policy.json` carries `approval_sources`; a source added upstream is absent from an old target's policy, and a missing block defaults to disabled, so the approval path is silently off. Both states pass `validate_shiki` and `doctor`.
  Why neither direction can simply be flipped: overwriting either file would destroy target-specific values. Writing `<file>.new` plus an explicit summary is what makes the difference visible without losing anything.
  Reproducible when: an upgrade of a target with an older config reports exactly which governance keys differ, leaves every project-content file intact, and refuses without writing anything when the target has pending migrations.

tasks.scope:
Write an install stamp into the target — a small JSON record naming the platform commit the install came from, the install timestamp, and a content digest per shipped path — and refresh it on every install and upgrade. It is target state, not a contract, so it belongs with the other target-owned records and must never be overwritten by a later install with older content.

Teach `shiki doctor` to report drift from it: a shipped path whose current content differs from the stamped digest (the target was hand-edited or half-upgraded), a stamp naming a platform commit that is not an ancestor of the running platform's HEAD (the target is ahead, or from a different lineage), and an absent stamp (a target installed before stamps existed — reported as a distinct finding, never as a pass). Drift must be a real doctor finding with its own id, so `--strict` fails on it.

Fix the migration target confusion: `shiki migrate` with `--target <other repo>` currently runs the PLATFORM's registry against the TARGET's state file, so it can write migration ids the target's own validator rejects, producing a permanently red required check. Either resolve the registry from the target's own `scripts/` when `--target` names a different repository, or refuse `--target` with a message telling the operator to run the target's own CLI. Refusing is acceptable and is the safer default; whichever is chosen must be covered by a test.

Add `tests/test_install_version_drift.py`: a fresh install writes a stamp; doctor reports no drift; editing one shipped file makes doctor report drift naming that path; removing the stamp produces the distinct absent-stamp finding, never a pass; `--strict` fails on drift; a stamp from a newer platform commit is reported rather than silently accepted; and `shiki migrate --target <other>` either uses the target's registry or refuses, asserted directly.

REPRODUCIBILITY — what this task removes, and what to change to get the same result.
  Symptom: you cannot tell an old target from a current one. A uniformly-old target is internally consistent, so `validate_shiki` passes and `doctor` reports zero failures — the same output a current target gives.
  Measured: `'VERSION' in TEMPLATE_PATHS` -> False; no Python file reads `VERSION` (only `.github/workflows/release.yml` mentions it); `shiki status` emits only `claude_command, codex_skill, command, config, root`; `shiki preflight` checks git-repo, GitHub-origin and `.shiki/repo.json` only; `shiki doctor` has no version check. The only instrument available today is diffing `TEMPLATE_PATHS` by hand against the platform.
  Second defect: the global `shiki` is a symlink into the platform checkout and `bin/shiki` execs the platform's `scripts/shiki.py`, so `shiki migrate --target <old target>` builds the registry from the PLATFORM and applies it to the TARGET's state file. `docs/releasing.md:145-149` shows the migrate commands with no `--target` at all, which is the only safe form.
  Reproducible when: doctor names the exact drifted paths in a hand-edited target, reports an absent stamp as its own finding, and `--strict` fails on both.
